claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is an as-cast or homogenized single-phase alloy.
Differential thermal expansion among the constituents of HfNbTaTiZr creates localized misfit strains.
Thermal-expansion-induced misfit strains produce localized residual stresses and lattice distortions.
The localized residual stresses impede or otherwise modify dislocation motion.
The localized residual stresses affect phase stability or phase evolution.
Changes in dislocation mobility and phase stability caused by residual thermal stresses govern the alloy's thermoelastic anomalies.
Changes in dislocation mobility and phase stability caused by residual thermal stresses govern the alloy's high-temperature creep behavior.
Changes in dislocation mobility and phase stability caused by residual thermal stresses govern cold-rolling and aging hardening.
A minor compositional substitution can be selected to reduce thermal expansion mismatch while approximately preserving elastic properties.
Reducing thermal expansion mismatch should produce a smoother temperature dependence of elastic moduli between 293 and 1100 K.
Reducing thermal expansion mismatch should diminish high-temperature creep anomalies at 1250 °C.
Reducing thermal expansion mismatch should diminish hardening associated with cold rolling.
Reducing thermal expansion mismatch should diminish hardening after aging at 600–800 °C.
The baseline HfNbTaTiZr alloy displays combined thermoelastic and mechanical anomalies.
The proposed mechanism is applicable from 293 K to 1250 °C.
A controlled comparison should hold testing conditions constant except for the compositional change intended to alter thermal expansion mismatch.
Failure of the modified alloy to alter the elastic-modulus, creep, and hardening anomalies relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
